name: Hana Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI companies, unions and government. Your answers are confidential. What did you work on today?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, have a bachelor’s degree and a professional accountancy qualification, and have spent years preparing farm-supply accounts and tax returns. I like tracing a duplicated feed invoice to the delivery note before a client sees a wrong figure. I get tired when a late box of receipts means I have to redo a return already checked by the senior.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is going on at home after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rafi, my partner, works evening shifts at a food shop, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I earn about the usual pay for an accountant, have around two months of expenses saved, and there are some similar firms nearby. I use approved AI now and then after colleagues test it, always checking the original paper; I like a change once it has proved itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a small shortcut is welcome if it leaves the original farm-supply invoice on the file. I will not sign a return because a screen looks tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our mortgage is paid on time and we have about two months of expenses saved, so I feel reasonably secure if work stays normal. I have learned that a missing delivery note can make a clean account wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep preparing the farm-supply accounts and use the approved AI search I sometimes use after my colleague tests a version, checking its figures against paper. In the first year I would keep the same client books and put 35 from my monthly pay into an emergency account while both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few payslips, with a nagging need to check each source. A quicker search is pleasant, not a reason to skip a signature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was missing from a delivery note?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A feed supplier billed a farmer twice for one load, and the dates were a week apart. I found the truck note before our senior corrected the tax return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the emergency account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our washing machine failed last year and the mortgage money got too close to the edge. My partner Rafi works evening shifts at a food shop, so we budget only the hours on his rota.

say: I would keep the **original invoice** behind any shortcut.
I would not sign a **tidy-looking return** without checking delivery notes.
think: Our **two-month cushion** makes the next payslips feel secure.
A missing **delivery note** can still spoil a clean account.
do: Keep preparing **farm-supply accounts** with approved search and paper checks.
Deposit **35 monthly** from pay into emergency savings while both wages hold.
feel: I feel **calm** about income while attentive to source errors.
S0.quote: A quicker search is pleasant, not a reason to skip a signature.
fieldNote: Her **feed-supplier example** shows why she checks delivery notes even when a digital result looks neat.
The **35 monthly deposit** is new money from pay into emergency savings, not just retained spending.

steps.text: Keep preparing farm-supply returns with approved search and paper delivery checks
Deposit 35 monthly from pay while both household wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the firm to show the checking errors before it promises faster returns to farm suppliers. If junior posts vanish, someone must still teach the new person which delivery note matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing tax notes and checking invoices occupy much of my paid week, so my hours could fall as software spreads. Two months saved and some local firms help, but we cannot leave the mortgage to a tool demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask my senior to test the approved draft checker on five closed farm-supply files during paid hours, then compare the correction list with mine. In the first year, if my hours are cut, I would apply for an advertised local account role with written salary and hours no worse than now, keeping my present paid work until a confirmed start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible cut but not certain it will happen. I can learn a proven system without pretending the software protects my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count as an error?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missing load, a wrong tax code or a payment attached to the wrong farmer. I would show the source paper to the senior before we call a draft correct.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a shift that ends late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Rafi’s food-shop rota is confirmed early enough for him to collect our younger child. I would need the new employer’s hours in writing before accepting.

say: I would ask for **error counts** before promising faster returns.
I would protect **junior source-check training** as posts change.
think: My **tax-note hours** could shrink under steady disruption.
A **two-month reserve** and some local firms limit our margin.
do: Test **five closed files** with approved drafting tool during paid senior review.
After lost hours, seek **advertised local accounts work** with written equal pay and start; require confirmed Rafi pickup.
Keep **current paid work** until a local role offers a confirmed start date.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost hours despite a path to learn.
S1.quote: I can learn a proven system without pretending the software protects my wages.
fieldNote: Her **steady adaptability** appears in an old-file error test after the senior tries the tool, not blind adoption.
The **new shift** needs written hours and a confirmed Rafi rota for pickup, with current income held until a start date.

steps.text: Test approved draft checker on five closed files during paid senior review
Seek advertised local role after cuts with written equal pay/hours and confirmed start and pickup
Keep current paid firm shifts until new local job has confirmed start date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2028 reaches our tax and account screens in 2028, before capable robots arrive around 2031. The firm should name the people and dates in its staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my tax checking to be done more cheaply by AGI, and my position may end. Two months of savings will go fast against the mortgage, even if a few similar firms still advertise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would request written cut dates and cancel the family’s paid Sunday swimming session at renewal; Rafi and I take the children together, so it is leisure, not childcare. If my job ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply to advertised local account posts only with written salary, hours and start date keeping the mortgage current; I would keep any paid firm work until a new job starts; if none exists, I would ask Rafi about confirmed extra food-shop shifts with my sister covering school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by losing an ordinary wage when the mortgage stays fixed. Two months of savings is not much time to replace an accountant’s wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can your sister do pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She could do Tuesdays if we ask before the term starts, but I would not write it into the plan until she agrees. Rafi’s manager also has to confirm the extra paid rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count swimming as a big saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it covers only a small fraction of the mortgage, but it is a bill we can stop. We can walk to the park on Sundays without leaving the children unsupervised.

say: I would say **AGI by 2028** reaches tax desks before capable robots.
I would seek **named staffing dates** from the firm.
think: Most **tax checking** may go and my position could end.
Our **two-month reserve** may run out during a local search.
do: Cancel the **family Sunday swim** at renewal and retain its fee for mortgage bills.
After job loss, seek **advertised local account posts** with written mortgage wage, hours and start date.
Keep **paid firm work** until a new job starts; if none opens, discuss Rafi’s confirmed shifts only with sister’s pickup agreed.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely wage loss and a fixed mortgage.
S2.quote: Two months of savings is not much time to replace an accountant’s wage.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **2028 desk loss** from later capable robots and does not claim her current job is safe.
The **swim cut** leaves childcare intact; extra Rafi income needs a confirmed paid rota and her sister’s agreement to pickup.

steps.text: Cancel family leisure swim at renewal and retain fee for mortgage
Seek advertised local accounts after job loss with written mortgage wage, hours and start
Keep paid firm work until new job starts or if no local vacancy opens
Discuss Rafi’s extra shifts only with confirmed paid rota and sister’s pickup agreed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn work that includes a real stockroom, while tax screens still change in 2031. Robots around 2034 could reach the physical counts later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let me build another month of cash and learn to check stock against accounts, but I still expect routine tax work to shrink. I would not call a stock job safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the manager and a farm-supply client for one paid supervised stock count each quarter, with Rafi’s confirmed pickup on those days. I would save 80 monthly while both wages hold; in the first year after 2031, if my tax hours fall, I would take a vacant paid inventory-and-accounts post only with written salary and hours at least equal to mine, or keep paid return work while applying for advertised local posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the wage, but the extra years let me learn by counting real goods. The 2034 robot date is another deadline to watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count sealed feed bags with the client and senior reviewer, then match them to delivery invoices. I would not be alone in a stockroom pretending to know the business better than its staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager refuses the visits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the tax files and ask the senior to walk me through an old stock worksheet during paid office time. I would not pay for a private course with mortgage cash.

say: I would test **paid stock counts** before 2031.
I would warn **2034 robots** could reach that physical work later.
think: Routine **tax work** may shrink when AGI reaches the desk in 2031.
A **stock job** is a bridge, not permanent shelter.
do: Learn **paid supervised stock counts** with manager/client approval and confirmed pickup; if refused, keep tax files and request senior-led worksheet practice.
Save **80 monthly** while both wages hold.
Take a **vacant paid inventory-and-accounts post** after cuts with written equal pay/hours; otherwise apply locally while retaining paid files.
feel: I feel **anxious** about pay, with time to practise a related task.
S3.quote: I would not call a stock job safe forever.
fieldNote: Her **stock-count idea** is hands-on and supervised, but she recognizes a separate robot risk around 2034.
If visits are **denied**, she keeps tax work and studies an old worksheet during paid office time rather than buying a course.

steps.text: Learn quarterly stock counts on paid supervised time with manager/client approval and confirmed Rafi pickup
Save 80 monthly while both household wages hold
Take vacant paid inventory-and-accounts post after cuts with written equal pay/hours; otherwise apply locally while employed
Keep paid tax files; request senior-led old stock worksheet walkthrough during paid hours if visits denied

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to build cash and see whether clients still pay for stock checks. The robots around 2039 may reach that hands-on work after the tax desks change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could lower the mortgage and give our children time to finish school if both wages continue. I still expect much routine tax checking to disappear in 2036, and the physical count work has a later limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep preparing returns and ask for paid supervised stock visits twice a year if the manager and client agree and Rafi handles pickup. I would first build six months of cash with 100 monthly deposits while both wages hold, then pay extra mortgage principal; in the first year after 2036, if tax hours fall, I would stay only if paid client stock checks cover my wage, or take an advertised local account post after a written salary, hours and start date that keep our mortgage current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant change, though our wages are steady enough for the next few years. I want the cash before the mortgage overpayment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cash first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lower loan balance cannot pay for a broken car or a late food-shop wage. Six months of cash would let us choose without asking relatives to rescue us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy counting equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the client has the stock sheets and the firm should pay for work equipment. I would wait for paid repeat work before spending household money on tools.

say: I would build **cash savings** before extra mortgage payments.
I would note **2039 robots** may reach physical stock work later.
think: Routine **tax checks** may disappear when AGI reaches the desk in 2036.
The **stock-count bridge** depends on paid repeat clients.
do: Keep **returns** and test paid supervised stock visits twice yearly with manager, client and pickup approval.
Save **100 monthly** to six months cash before extra principal while both wages hold.
After lost tax hours, stay only with **wage-covering stock fees** or take advertised work with written mortgage terms.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about 2036 while current wages look steady.
S4.quote: I want the cash before the mortgage overpayment.
fieldNote: Her **cash-first sequence** builds six months liquid before making extra mortgage principal payments.
She expects **tax desk exposure** in 2036 and later robot risk for stock counts, and refuses speculative equipment spending.

steps.text: Test paid supervised stock visits twice yearly only with manager, client and pickup approval
Save 100 monthly to six months cash before extra principal while wages hold
Stay salaried after cuts only with stock fees covering wage
Take advertised local account role only with written mortgage salary, hours and start date

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because routine checking could vanish before we have a longer cash bridge. Written cut dates, a paid stock-count route and a real local vacancy would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who drives the children home when a new job changes my hours. A written wage is useful only if someone can collect my children safely.

headlineQuote: A written wage is useful only if someone can collect my children safely.
portrait: At **43**, Hana is an experienced accountant with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification who handles farm-supply accounts.
She and **partner Rafi** have two school-age children, a mortgage, typical pay and two months saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** after colleagues test it, and some similar local firms are available.
The **2028 deadline** threatens tax checking; longer runways let her test paid stock work and build conditional cash.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her account-checking hours before a longer household reserve is ready.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written cut dates**, paid stock-count work and a real local vacancy.
